zh.title: 小引 · 一本书，和一册书
zh.deck: 先认识《随笔集》，再翻开蒙田留在自己那册印本上的笔迹。

sections.heading: 一本书
paragraphs: 蒙田是十六世纪的法国人。一五七〇年，他离开了公职；次年，三十八岁的他宣布退居自己的庄园。塔楼里的书房后来成了他写作的地方。他没有从此闭门不出，外面的事务也没有就此放过他。不过，一本书在这里慢慢长了出来。
这本书不成体系。它由长短不一的一篇篇文章组成，题目随手得很：论悔，论虚妄，论经验，论醉酒，论驿站。想到哪儿写到哪儿，中间夹着大量古人的话。
书名是他自己起的。法文那个词有试一试、掂量一番的意思，像拿不准而去称一称。后来，它成了一个体裁的名字；在那之前，它先是这本书的名字。
他试的对象是他自己。
这书写了许多年，也长了许多年。一五八〇年头一回出版，两卷。一五八八年的题名页标作第五版，称添了六百处，另加第三卷。全书至此一百零七章。
一五八八年那一版印出来之后，他没有停。

sections.heading: 一册书
paragraphs: 他手上那一册一五八八年的印本传了下来，如今藏在波尔多的图书馆里，人称波尔多本。
此后几年，直到一五九二年去世，他还在这一册上写写划划。页边有，行间有，压在原字上头的也有。
所以这一册书上，可以先认出两层。印出来的是一层，是一五八八年那一版的样子；手写的是另一层，是那以后陆续留下的修改。手写这一层内部还有早晚，不是一回落成的。今天翻开它，印字与笔迹都在眼前。
这是一件难得的东西。我们通常读到的是改定后的文字，看不见先前的说法怎样退了场。而他没有另起一本，就在自己那册印好的书上接着写。于是，后来想的和先前印的，留在同一张纸上。
有一件事得先说明。他死后三年，另有一版《随笔集》出版，跟这一册不尽相同。两者的关系牵涉一场复杂的版本讨论。这里不替那场讨论下结论，只从这一册上能够辨认的印字、增补与删改说起。

sections.heading: 下面五篇
paragraphs: 下面五篇，讲的都是这一册书让我们看见的事：他写下了什么，后来又回去动了什么，哪一句他留着，哪一句他自己划了。纸能告诉我们的，有时比我们以为的多，有时又少得多。
每篇另有一则旁注，拿一个当代的框架跟他并排放一下，那个框架叫 SAE。旁注是旁注，不是论证，也不主张谁从谁那里来。可以跳过不读。

notes: 以一五八八年波尔多本为主要观察对象；不据此裁定它与一五九五年版的先后及权威关系。文中译述以行文通顺为先，不作逐字对译。

en.title: A Book, and One Particular Copy
en.deck: An introduction to the Essays—and to the printed pages on which Montaigne kept writing.

sections.heading: The book
paragraphs: Montaigne was a sixteenth-century Frenchman. He left public office in 1570. The following year, at thirty-eight, he announced his retirement to his estate. A room in its tower became his study. This was no permanent disappearance from the world: he travelled, and public duties would find him again. But a book began to grow there.

It was not a system. It consisted of pieces of very different lengths, with titles that could sound almost casual: Of Repentance, Of Vanity, Of Experience, Of Drunkenness, Of Post-horses. One thought led to another, with the voices of ancient writers joining him along the way.
He called the book Essais: attempts, trials, acts of weighing something up. The word would become the name of a literary form. Before that, it was the name of his book.
What he was trying out was himself.

He worked on it for years, and it kept growing. The first edition appeared in 1580, in two books. The title page of the 1588 edition called it the fifth, advertised six hundred additions, and announced a third book. There were now 107 chapters.
Publication did not bring the writing to an end.

sections.heading: The copy
paragraphs: One copy of that 1588 edition—the copy Montaigne continued to work in—has survived. It is held in the library in Bordeaux and is known as the Bordeaux Copy.
He kept annotating it during the remaining years of his life, until his death in 1592. There is writing in the margins, between the lines, and over the printed letters themselves.

At first glance, there are two layers. One is print: the book as it stood in 1588. The other is handwriting: what he subsequently added, deleted, or altered. That second layer has its own earlier and later moments; it was not put down all at once. Open the volume now, and print and pen are both before you.

Usually we meet a revised passage after the old wording has gone. Here, Montaigne carried on inside the book already printed. What he had published and what he went on to think remain on the same sheet of paper.

One qualification belongs at the beginning. Another edition appeared in 1595, three years after his death, and its text differs from this copy. The relationship between the two is a complex editorial question. These essays will not settle it. They begin with the printed words and handwritten interventions that can be made out on these pages.

sections.heading: The five essays that follow
paragraphs: The following pieces look at what this particular copy allows us to see: what Montaigne wrote, what he returned to, what he left standing, and what he crossed out. Sometimes the paper tells us more than we expect. Sometimes it tells us considerably less.

Each essay also has a separate aside, placing a contemporary framework called SAE alongside the passage. An aside is not a proof, and this comparison makes no claim of intellectual descent. You can leave the asides unread.

notes: These essays take the 1588 Bordeaux Copy as their principal object, without deciding its priority or authority in relation to the 1595 edition. Montaigne's words are rendered freely for the purposes of the essays.

zh.title: 他把一个问号放进了铭里
zh.deck: 一句怀疑自己的话，怎样成了他愿意随身携带的铭。

sections.heading: 全书最长的那一章
paragraphs: 《随笔集》第二卷第十二章叫《雷蒙·塞邦辩护》。它是全书最长的一章，一章就抵得上一本小书。
题目说是辩护。塞邦是十五世纪的一位学者，写过一本书，用人世间的道理去讲教门的事。蒙田的父亲让他把这本书译成法文。后来有人挑这本书的毛病，他写了这一章替它挡。
而他挡的办法，是把人靠道理去确定什么的本事整个拆一遍。拆到什么地步，下一篇再说。这一篇只看拆完之后，他给自己留了什么。

sections.heading: 那批人的难处
paragraphs: 章子中段，他替一批怀疑者记了一笔账。他们不肯轻易断定，可他们得开口。一开口，麻烦就来了。
有人堵他们：你们说我不知道，这一句你知道不知道。
这一堵堵在要害上。我什么都不知道，听上去仍是一句断言。要把一切知识都撤掉，它似乎得先把自己也算进去；若给它自己留个例外，又凭什么留。
蒙田记下了他们怎样脱身。他们说，这句话把自己连同别的一起带走。跟着他给了一个药铺里的比喻：大黄这一味，把坏东西泻出去，也把自己泻出去。
这个比喻好在不含糊。它没有替那句话取得一个永远站得住的位置。它说的是，那句话干完活，也得走人。

sections.heading: 他把它领回了自己家
paragraphs: 这一段本来是在替别人记账。那批人的难处，那批人的脱身法，他是记下来的那一个。
而记着记着，他说了一句自己的话：这个念头换一种说法更稳当，就是把它问出来。
Que sais-je？我知道什么呢？
跟着是更少见的一件事。他说，他把这一句携作自己的铭，配上一枚天平的图样。

sections.heading: 铭是个什么位子
paragraphs: 铭像是挂在门楣上的东西。
家训也好，堂号也好，座右铭也好，这一类话通常要替人认下一点什么。要立得住，要经得起挂上去许多年，要让进门的人一眼看见你认什么。
他却把一个问题放在了那个位子上。
天平也配得上。它让两边暂时悬着，等着称量。在这里，它不像一枚宣告胜负的印章，更像是把判断再留一会儿。

sections.heading: 他后来动过这一句吗
paragraphs: 这就要看波尔多本了：他自己那一册一五八八年的印本，上头留着此后几年的笔迹。
Que sais-je 那一句在印面上，手写的那一层没有动它。而紧挨着它的下半句，他动了。印面原是 Voyla comme je la porte，他把头一个词 Voyla 划掉了。
笔到了它旁边，却没有把这个问题撤走。留下，不等于替它作了一次新的宣誓。但这个距离仍然值得停一下：他回来过，而这句话还在。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 问句省事，也不省事。
它不再把我一无所知当作一条确定的知识来宣布，因而避开了刚才那种直接的自撞。可这并不使它免于追问。它为什么问，问到哪里停，又拿什么去生活，都还在后面。
他没有说自己赢了。他把问题配在一枚天平上。天平暂时悬着，而不是替他把事情结清。

zh.aside: 当代有一个叫 SAE 的框架，用的是一把相近的测试：看一句反对，能不能不做它所反对的那件事就说完。它拿这把测试去找那条撤不掉的，蒙田在这里则退开了断言的形式。同一件工具，一个用来留，一个用来退。这只是并读，不是说谁从谁那里来，也不是把两者当作同一套论证。
notes: 据《随笔集》II.12《雷蒙·塞邦辩护》译述。问句的作用不等于不可反驳；篇末区分文字的保留与作者持续认同。

en.title: A Question for a Motto
en.deck: Montaigne found a sentence he could carry with him. It did not tell anyone what to believe.

sections.heading: The longest chapter
paragraphs: The twelfth chapter of Book II of the Essays is called An Apology for Raymond Sebond. It is the longest chapter in the work: a small book inside a much larger one.

The title promises a defence. Sebond was a fifteenth-century scholar who had written a book reasoning from the human world towards matters of faith. Montaigne's father asked him to translate it into French. When critics attacked the book, Montaigne took up its defence.

His method was to take apart the human capacity for arriving at certainty through reason. How far he carried this will be the subject of the next essay. Here, the question is what he kept for himself when the work was done.

sections.heading: The trouble with saying it
paragraphs: Partway through the chapter, Montaigne describes a difficulty faced by the sceptics. They are unwilling to make a firm pronouncement. But they still have to speak. As soon as they do, someone can interrupt.
You say you do not know. Do you know that?

The objection finds a vulnerable point. I know nothing still sounds like a claim to knowledge. If every claim is to be withdrawn, this one seems to belong in the same pile. If it is to be spared, on what grounds?

Montaigne records their answer. The statement carries itself away along with everything else. He gives it an image from the apothecary's shop: rhubarb, the purgative that expels what is unwanted and is itself expelled.
The force of the image lies in what it does not promise. The sentence is not being awarded a permanent place above the argument. Once it has done its work, it has to go too.

sections.heading: He brings it home
paragraphs: Until this point, Montaigne has been keeping an account of other people's predicament: the trap they found themselves in, and the way they tried to escape it.
Then he speaks for himself. The thought would be more securely expressed, he says, as a question.
Que sais-je? What do I know?
And he does something more unusual still. He tells us that he carries this question as his motto, accompanied by the image of a balance.

sections.heading: Where a motto belongs
paragraphs: A motto belongs, figuratively, over the door.
Whether it is a family maxim or a personal watchword, it usually commits its owner to something. It must bear being displayed for years. It tells whoever enters what the household stands for.
Montaigne gives that place to a question.
The balance suits it. Its two pans can remain suspended while the weighing continues. Here it looks less like a seal announcing victory than a way of keeping a judgment open.

sections.heading: Did he return to it?
paragraphs: For that, we turn to the Bordeaux Copy: Montaigne's own copy of the 1588 edition, bearing the marks of the years that followed.
The printed Que sais-je remains unchanged. But in the words immediately following it, Voyla comme je la porte, he crossed out Voyla.

His pen reached the neighbouring words without removing the question. Leaving a sentence in place is not the same as renewing an oath to it. Still, the distance is worth noticing: he came back to this spot, and the question remained.

sections.heading: What the question leaves open
paragraphs: A question makes one thing easier and leaves other things difficult.

It no longer announces I know nothing as a certain piece of knowledge, and so avoids that particular collision with itself. But it is not beyond scrutiny. Why ask? Where does the asking stop? How does one live while the answer remains unsettled?
Montaigne does not tell us he has won. He places his question beside a balance. The pans remain suspended. They do not settle his account for him.

en.aside: A contemporary framework called SAE uses a related test: can an objection be stated without performing the very thing it objects to? SAE uses the test to seek what cannot be withdrawn. Montaigne, here, steps back from the form of assertion. A similar instrument is put to different work: one seeks something to retain, the other a way to retreat. This is a juxtaposition, not a claim of descent or an assertion that the two arguments are identical.
notes: Based on Essays II.12, rendered freely. Turning an assertion into a question does not make it immune to criticism; a sentence left on the page does not, by itself, establish continuing assent.

zh.title: 你得先丢掉自己的武器
zh.deck: 一种反驳能把对手逼到尽头，也会把使用它的人带进去。

paragraphs: 上一篇说到，《雷蒙·塞邦辩护》是替一本书挡的，而蒙田挡的办法，是把人的道理整个拆一遍。这一篇看他怎么拆，以及他自己知不知道这一拆要花什么。

sections.heading: 两拨人，第二拨更难对付
paragraphs: 挑塞邦毛病的有两拨。头一拨质疑的是信仰何须人的道理来扶持；第二拨说的是：塞邦讲的那些道理不结实。
蒙田答第二拨用的办法，他写在明处，一点没藏：把他们理性那一点可怜的武器从手里夺走。
跟着他问了一句。这一句一出，事情的规模就变了：那就看看，人是不是有比塞邦更强的道理，乃至他究竟能不能靠论证和推理到达任何确定的东西。
不是塞邦的道理结不结实，是人的道理能不能结实。
这一问出来，麻烦跟着来了。塞邦讲的也是人的道理。人的道理要是到不了确定的地方，塞邦那一本自然也不能单靠这些道理到达。
他替塞邦挡住了那些人，同时把塞邦在这一场争论里站的那块地也挖了。
有一处得说清楚，不然容易读成他把塞邦整个否了。他拆的是单凭人世的道理能不能确定什么。信从那一头，他在这一章里另有交代，不在这一拆的范围内。他自己划的界就是这么划的：只凭人的武器，看能走多远。

sections.heading: 他没有站在坑外面
paragraphs: 写到后来，他有一句：我们把这个人摆在他自己面前，把他的理性摆在他的理性面前，看它能说出什么来。
结论他也写了：圆规连同用圆规的那一个，一起归零。
不是只有那件量东西的工具归零，拿它来量的那个人也一起。说话的人没有给自己留一个站在外面的位子。

sections.heading: 他掉过头去，说了价钱
paragraphs: 紧接着，他不再只对着挑毛病的人说话了。
写到这里，他转向一位夫人。他说，自己为她破了例，写了这么长的一篇。然后是这几句：这最后一手，只能当极药用。这是一记绝望的招法，你得先丢掉自己的武器，才能让对手丢掉他的。这是个秘招，要少用，要留着用。
他还给了一句更短的：这是为了毁掉对方而毁掉你自己。
跟着，他劝她照平常那样替你的塞邦说话就好。
要留意，他说的不是别用。他说的是，这一手有价钱，所以要挑时候。

sections.heading: 一句人人使过的话
paragraphs: 吵架的时候，有一句话很好使：你还不是一样。
它常常是真的，所以对方一时答不上来。可它干的事其实很有限：它把说话的人拉回他自己立的那把尺子里，让他不能站在尺子外头发话。
它并没有证明那把尺子不成立。迟到的人说迟到耽误事，他自己迟到不假，话却不因此变假。
蒙田这一手不能就当作一句你还不是一样。他要追问的是，那把用来取得确定性的尺子到底靠不靠得住。可两者有一点相通：你不能只把对方送进去，自己留在外面。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 在全书最长的这一章里，他把人的确定性逼到了尽头，也转过身，对那位夫人说：这个办法别常用，照老法子替他说话就行。
一个人把自己的办法用到这样的地步，还肯告诉身边的人它有多贵。这不只是谦。他知道这一手要花掉什么，也知道那笔钱不是每回都付得起。
极药之所以是极药，不只在药性猛，还在于吃下去的人也得承受它。

zh.aside: SAE 是个当代的框架，它把不给自己留例外立成一条纪律，写得很干脆。蒙田在这一章里也不把自己排除在检验之外，写到后来又报了价钱：这一手，你得先丢掉自己的武器，所以要省着用。纪律那边写的是该怎么做，他这边留下的是做了要花什么。两样并排放着，不必谁去解释谁。
notes: 据《随笔集》II.12译述。文中的拆解限于单凭人的理性取得确定性的主张，不据此把蒙田的信仰立场一并化约。

en.title: You Have to Drop Your Own Weapons
en.deck: Montaigne takes an argument as far as it will go, then tells its intended user what it costs.

paragraphs: The previous essay left Montaigne defending a book by dismantling the human claim to certainty. This one asks how he does it—and whether he knows what his method will cost.

sections.heading: The harder objection
paragraphs: Sebond's critics fall into two groups. The first questions the need to support faith with human reasoning at all. The second says that Sebond's reasoning is simply not good enough.
Montaigne makes no secret of his answer to the second group. He proposes to take the meagre weapons of reason out of their hands.
Then he asks a question that enlarges the dispute. Do they have better arguments than Sebond? Can a human being, by argument and inference alone, arrive at anything certain?
The issue is no longer whether Sebond's reasons are sound. It is whether human reasoning can stand securely at all.

The difficulty is immediate. Sebond uses human reasoning too. If reasoning cannot reach certainty on its own, his book cannot reach it by that route either. Montaigne has held off the attackers by digging away the ground on which Sebond, in this particular contest, also stands.

A boundary matters here. This is not the same as rejecting Sebond outright. Montaigne is testing what unaided human reason can establish; faith has a separate place in the chapter. The trial is being conducted with human weapons. The question is how far those weapons will take us.

sections.heading: No safe place outside
paragraphs: Later, Montaigne proposes that we place this human being before himself, and his reason before his reason, to see what it has to say.
He supplies the outcome too. The compasses and the person wielding them are both brought to nothing.
It is not only the measuring instrument that fails the test. The measurer goes with it. The person making the argument has reserved no safe patch of ground beyond its reach.

sections.heading: Then he names the price
paragraphs: At this point in the chapter, Montaigne turns from the critics to a woman he is addressing. For her, he says, he has broken his usual practice and written at such length.

What follows is a warning. This last move is an extreme remedy. It is a desperate stroke: you must abandon your own weapons to make your opponent abandon his. Such a secret method should be used sparingly, and held in reserve.
He gives it an even shorter description. You destroy yourself in order to destroy the other person.
Then he advises her to go on defending her Sebond in the ordinary way.
Notice what he does not say. He does not forbid the method. He says that it has a price, and that one should choose the occasion.

sections.heading: You do it too
paragraphs: There is a useful line in an argument: you do it too.

Often it is true, which may leave the other person briefly speechless. But its achievement is limited. It places the speaker back under the standard they have applied to someone else. They cannot stand outside their own rule.
It does not show that the rule is wrong. Someone who is habitually late can still be right that lateness wastes other people's time.

Montaigne's argument is not merely a grander version of you do it too. He is asking whether the instrument used to establish certainty can be trusted in the first place. There is, nevertheless, a shared requirement: you cannot send your opponent into the test and arrange to stay outside it yourself.

sections.heading: An extreme remedy
paragraphs: In the longest chapter of his book, Montaigne presses the claim to human certainty to its limit. He also turns to the woman he is addressing and says: do not make a habit of this. Defend him in the usual way.

A man carries his own method this far and still tells someone close to the argument how expensive it is. This is more than modesty. He knows what using it requires. He knows the price cannot be paid on every occasion.
An extreme remedy is not extreme only because it is powerful. The person who takes it must also endure it.

en.aside: The contemporary framework SAE makes refusing an exemption for oneself an explicit discipline. Montaigne, too, includes himself in the test. What he also supplies is the cost: you have to drop your own weapons, so use the method sparingly. On one side is a statement of how to proceed; on the other, an account of what proceeding requires. They can be set beside each other without making either explain the other away.
notes: Based on Essays II.12, rendered freely. The argument concerns certainty obtained through unaided human reason; it is not treated here as a complete statement of Montaigne's religious position.

zh.title: 他把退路划了
zh.deck: 页边一句写下又划掉的话，留下了一条不能轻易替他走完的解释。

paragraphs: 蒙田的《随笔集》第三卷第二章叫《论悔》。开篇，他写了一句很少有人愿意写的话：这个人要是让我重做一遍，我会做得很不一样；可事情已经这样了。
这一章要办的是个麻烦事。一个人写一本讲自己的书，写了许多年，中间他自己变了。那书里写的到底是谁？
而波尔多本让我们看见，他怎样在这些话上继续动手。那是他本人用过的一册印本，上头留着生前最后几年的笔迹。

sections.heading: 边栏上那一句
paragraphs: 《论悔》的左边栏上，他写过一句话：退一万步，在这么多变来变去的形状里头，你就挑那个变得最少的。
这句话里有一个补在行上的小字，a。而整条边注，又被划掉了。
这句话没有印在一五八八年的正文里；它被添在页边，又被删除。如今我们还能读它，却不能把它当作他在这里最后留下的正文。
它很像一条讲得通的退路：变来变去没关系，总有一样变得慢一些，把那一样认作你。
这样读，删线就显得重了。不过，重的是这一种读法。纸能证明他撤去了这句话，不能单凭一道线，就证明他为什么撤去，或者他已拒绝了哪一种关于自己的哲学。

sections.heading: 它所在的那一段
paragraphs: 这一章开头，还有最有名的几行。
他先说，这世上没有一样东西是不动的，恒常本身也不过是一种懒一点的摇晃。跟着说，我没法把我的对象定住，它昏昏沉沉、东倒西歪，像天生带着醉意。我只能就它当下这个样子，在我盯着它看的那一刻，把它接下来。
然后是那两句：我画的不是存在。我画的是经过。
不是从一个年纪到另一个年纪的那种经过，也不是人们说的七年一变，是一天一天，一分钟一分钟。

sections.heading: 他后来回来动过它
paragraphs: 这些话在一五八八年的印面上已经有了。波尔多本上，又留下他改动这几行标点和大小写的笔迹。
字母提了上去，标点动过了。他回到那些已经印好的话里，重新安排句子的停顿。
一个刚说自己抓不住对象的人，回过头来重新整理句子的边界。这是纸上动作给人的印象，不必把它升成他的自我解释。对象在动，句子仍可以再写得准确一点。

sections.heading: 一件人人做过的事
paragraphs: 翻出自己几年前写的东西，要是起了改的念头，会卡在同一个地方。改了，那段文字就不再原样保着当年的写法；不改，它就一直挂在那儿，写着一些你现在不那么想的话。
折中的办法是有的：把看着刺眼的字眼磨圆一点，别的留着。磨圆的地方是新的那一层，底下压着的还是旧的。
蒙田留下的这一册，让这种两难有了一个看得见的样子。修改发生了，旧的那一层却没有全被盖掉。今天翻开它，两层都还在。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 他在这一章开头说过，这个人要是让我重做一遍，我会做得很不一样；可事情已经这样了。
在同一章的页边，那句挑那个变得最少的，写下了，又划去了。
我们可以把它读作一条出现过、又没有留下的退路。但别越过那道线，替他宣布一个终于找到的答案。他留下来的，仍是一个不能被定住的人，和一本还在动的书。

zh.aside: SAE 的意义论里，有两句话可以放到这一处旁边。一句说，没有预制的真我，也没有完成的真我，而理由是反身，不是时间。另一句说，一个人拿什么姿态对自己，没有正面的判据，只有一条底线：不伪造一份圆满。按这一条线索，我们可以把那句写下又划去的话读成一份未被保留的圆满。但这只是并读的方向，不是删线已经替我们证明了蒙田的动机。
notes: 据《随笔集》III.2《论悔》译述。将删句读作退路，是本文的解释；删除事实本身不足以证明思想动机。

en.title: The Way Out He Crossed Out
en.deck: A deleted sentence offers a tempting explanation. The line through it does not prove that explanation.

paragraphs: Near the opening of Of Repentance, the second chapter of Book III, Montaigne says something few people readily say about themselves. If he had this person to make again, he would make him very differently. But it is done now.
The chapter has a difficult job. A man has spent years writing a book about himself. During those years, the man has changed. Who, then, is the person in the book?
The Bordeaux Copy lets us see him continuing to work on the question. This is the printed volume he used in the last years of his life, with his later writing still upon it.

sections.heading: A sentence in the margin
paragraphs: In the left margin of Of Repentance, Montaigne wrote a sentence whose thought is this: if all else fails, among so many changing forms, choose the one that changes least.
There is a small word, a, inserted above its line. The whole marginal sentence is crossed out.
The sentence was not part of the printed text of 1588. It was added by hand and then struck out. We can still read it, but we cannot treat it as the wording he finally left in place here.
It sounds like a reasonable escape. Everything may change, but surely something changes more slowly than the rest. Let that be you.

Read it that way, and the cancellation acquires weight. But the weight belongs to an interpretation. The paper can show that he withdrew a sentence. A line through the words cannot, on its own, show why he withdrew them, or which philosophy of the self he had decided to reject.

sections.heading: The passage around it
paragraphs: The chapter opens with some of Montaigne's best-known lines.

Nothing in the world stays still, he says. Even constancy is a slower kind of movement. He cannot fix his subject in place: it staggers and sways as though drunk by nature. He can take it only as it is at the instant he looks.
He does not portray being. He portrays passing.
Not the passage from one age of life to the next, nor some change counted in seven-year intervals. Day by day. Minute by minute.

sections.heading: He comes back to the sentences
paragraphs: These words were already in the printing of 1588. The Bordeaux Copy shows Montaigne returning to their punctuation and capitals.
A letter becomes a capital; a punctuation mark is altered. He goes back into the words already printed and rearranges the places where a reader pauses.

A man who has just said that he cannot hold his subject still goes back to reconsider where his sentences end. That is an impression the marks invite, not a self-explanation they require us to put into his mouth. The subject keeps moving. The sentences can still be made more exact.

sections.heading: Something we have all done
paragraphs: Find something you wrote a few years ago, and the wish to revise it can catch you in the same place. Change it, and it no longer preserves exactly how you wrote then. Leave it alone, and it continues to say things you no longer quite believe.
A compromise is possible. Soften the word that now offends you. Leave the rest. The softened place belongs to the new layer; the older writing remains underneath.
Montaigne's copy gives this difficulty a visible form. Revision happened, but the earlier layer was not entirely concealed. Open the book today, and both are still there.

sections.heading: What remains
paragraphs: At the beginning of the chapter, Montaigne says that if he could make this man again, he would make him differently. But it is done now.
In the margin of the same chapter, the proposal to choose what changes least was written down and crossed out.

We may read it as a way out that appeared and was not retained. But we should not cross the line ourselves and announce, on his behalf, a final answer. What remains is a person who cannot be fixed in place, and a book still being changed.

en.aside: Two propositions from SAE's account of meaning can be placed beside this page. There is neither a ready-made true self nor a completed true self; the reason is reflexivity, not simply the passage of time. And there is no positive test for the right stance towards oneself, only a lower limit: do not fabricate a finished wholeness. Along this line of reading, the cancelled sentence might look like a wholeness proposed and not retained. That is a possible juxtaposition. The cancellation does not establish Montaigne's motive for us.
notes: Based on Essays III.2, rendered freely. The description of the deleted sentence as a way out is an interpretation, not a conclusion established by the act of deletion alone.

zh.title: 我只增添，不修改
zh.deck: 一条印出来的规矩，和留在同一册书上的删改。

paragraphs: 《随笔集》第三卷第九章叫《论虚妄》。第三卷本身是新添的一卷；写到这里，蒙田又让自己的试写往前走一段，称这是第三次续。跟着，他给自己立了一条规矩。
我只增添，不修改。
理由他也给了。把自己的活抵押给了世人的那个人，我看他就不再有权处置它了。他要是能说得更好，换个地方去说，别糟蹋他已经卖掉的那一件。
这句话和读者手上新添的这一卷正好照着：他说我只增添，而这一卷就是增添。增添本来就在规矩允许的范围里。

sections.heading: 同一段里
paragraphs: 这句话印在一五八八年那一版上。而波尔多本上，同一段里就有他后来落的笔。
给完理由的那一句，原来说的是别糟蹋他卖给我们的那件活。我们，nous。这个词被他划掉了。
变化很小，也很具体：卖掉的那件东西还在，买下它的我们从句子里退出了。不是隔了许多章才出现另一种动作。笔就在这一段里面。

sections.heading: 不止一种动笔
paragraphs: 这册书上的动笔，不只是往空白处添话。上一篇已经见过，一条后来写上的边注，被他取消了。下一篇还会看见，就在《论虚妄》里，他把一条印出来的句子重新写过。
可这些动作也不能混在一起。一处标点改写，一句撤去的判断，一段另起的补充，不是同一种事情。问题不在纸上留下了多少墨水，而在笔究竟做了什么。

sections.heading: 他说的修改是哪一种
paragraphs: 这里要慢一点。
他说不修改，随后给的理由是：作品已经交出去了，若能说得更好，就到别处去说，别糟蹋已交出去的那一件。这不只是说一句话有没有语病，也关乎一个人还能怎样处置自己的旧作。
所以，拿标点变动去数他违约了多少次，数得再准，也未必对题。添上一段新话更不能自动算作反证，因为他明说自己允许增添。
真正留下张力的，是对已经印出的文字所做的删除和替换。只是，即便看见这些，也还要问：他所说的修改，和我们今天把这些动作归在一起的叫法，边界是否完全一样？纸不会替我们省下这个问题。

sections.heading: 那句话还在，笔迹也还在
paragraphs: 有三件事得分开，不然容易一笔带过。
第一，是历史上的那句话。他确实写下过我只增添，不修改，而且印了出去。后来无论他做了什么，这件事不会消失。
第二，是他后来还怎样认它。一句话没被划掉，只说明它还在书里，不说明他每一天都按当初同样的分量认着它。
第三，是他实际怎样动笔。增添、删除、替换，在书页上各有痕迹。能辨认清楚的动作，就说到动作；它在他心里算作什么，不能顺手替他补上。
三件事一旦揉在一起，就很容易读出一个现成的自相矛盾的人。更老实的说法是：规矩在，删改也在。它们能否被同一个说法安放，不因为两样都看见了，就自动结清。

sections.heading: 墙上那张表
paragraphs: 这类情形，在家里也见过。
贴过一张作息表，或者一份训练计划，写得很清楚。过了半年，人早不照着做了，而那张表还在墙上。
有时，撕掉它像是认了输；照着做又做不到。于是它就挂着，人从底下走过去，一天几回。也有时，它不过是被忘在那儿。旁人只看见那张纸，不能替屋主把这两种情形分清。
这不是拿家里的那张表解释蒙田。它只是提醒我们，同样一件留下的东西，可以有不同的留法。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 不是没有立过规矩。他把规矩印成了字，也把删改留成了笔迹。两样摊在同一册书上，谁也没有把谁遮掉。
这已经足够让人停下来，却还不够让我们替他判完那笔账。

zh.aside: SAE 的意义论给一种情形留了专门的名字，叫当作史：一个人在自己心里按已经做成来算，而实际上并没有在自己那里做成的那些条目。那句我只增添，不修改，会不会落在这本账上？要回答，不只得看他做过什么，还得知道他后来在自己那里怎样认这句话。这个条件，我们不能单靠它没有被划掉来补足。旁注可以把问题放到这里，不能代替蒙田判账。
notes: 据《随笔集》III.9《论虚妄》译述。增添符合所引规则，不作为反证；这里只讨论删除、替换与该规则之间尚待解释的张力。

en.title: I Add; I Do Not Correct
en.deck: A printed rule and a working copy full of changes occupy the same pages.

paragraphs: Of Vanity is the ninth chapter of Book III of the Essays. Book III is itself a new addition. Montaigne invites his attempt to run on a little further, calling this its third continuation. Then he states a rule for himself.
He adds. He does not correct.

He explains why. Once a man has pledged his work to the public, Montaigne thinks he no longer has the right to dispose of it at will. If he can say something better, let him say it somewhere else. He should not spoil the thing he has already sold.
The declaration fits the new book the reader is holding. He says he adds, and here is the addition. Adding is expressly allowed.

sections.heading: In the same paragraph
paragraphs: The rule was printed in 1588. In the Bordeaux Copy, the same paragraph also carries his later pen marks.
The sentence about the work already sold originally included us: the work he has sold us. Montaigne crossed out nous.

The change is small and exact. The thing sold remains in the sentence; we, its purchasers, have stepped out. There is no need to turn through many chapters before a different kind of action appears. The pen is already at work inside this paragraph.

sections.heading: Different uses of the pen
paragraphs: Writing in this copy did not only mean filling blank spaces. The previous essay looked at a marginal sentence that was added and then cancelled. The next will turn to another passage in Of Vanity where Montaigne rewrote a sentence already in print.

But these interventions should not all be treated alike. A changed punctuation mark, a withdrawn judgment, and a new passage of explanation are different actions. The question is not how much ink has reached the paper. It is what the pen has done.

sections.heading: What counts as correcting?
paragraphs: It is worth slowing down here.

Montaigne's reason for leaving the old work alone concerns something already handed over to others. If he can do better, he should do it elsewhere. This is more than a remark about faulty wording. It concerns what an author may still do with work that has left his hands.

Counting punctuation changes as breaches of contract may therefore miss the point, however accurately one counts them. Nor can a newly added paragraph automatically be evidence against his rule. He has said that additions are permitted.

The tension lies in deleting or replacing words already in print. Even then, a question remains: does what he means by correcting have precisely the same boundaries as the category into which we now place these actions? The page does not spare us that question.

sections.heading: Three things to keep apart
paragraphs: First, there is the historical statement. Montaigne wrote that he added but did not correct, and he published it. Nothing he later did can make that event unhappen.

Second, there is his later relationship to the statement. A sentence not crossed out is a sentence still in the book. That alone does not tell us that he continued to endorse it, every day, with the same meaning and force.

Third, there are his actions. Additions, deletions, and replacements have left distinguishable marks. Where we can identify an action, we should describe it. We should not quietly add an account of what he thought that action amounted to.

Compress these three matters into one, and a ready-made self-contradictory author appears. A more careful account is less conclusive. The rule is there. So are the alterations. Seeing both does not, by itself, reconcile them or close the case.

sections.heading: The plan on the wall
paragraphs: Something like this is familiar at home.
A daily schedule or a training plan goes up on the wall. The instructions are perfectly clear. Six months later, no one follows them, but the sheet is still there.

Sometimes taking it down would feel like admitting defeat, while following it is beyond reach. So it stays, and its owner walks past it several times a day. Sometimes it has simply been forgotten. A visitor who sees only the paper cannot tell those situations apart.
This is not an explanation of Montaigne. It is a reminder that the same thing can remain in place in more than one way.

sections.heading: The account stays open
paragraphs: He did set down a rule. He also left alterations in ink. Both lie in the same copy, neither hiding the other.
That is enough to make us pause. It is not enough to let us settle the account on his behalf.

en.aside: SAE's account of meaning names a particular kind of record: things a person counts, in their own understanding, as accomplished when they have not actually accomplished them there. Could Montaigne's claim to add without correcting belong in that record? We would need to know not only what he did, but how he subsequently held the claim in his own understanding. The fact that he did not cross it out cannot supply that missing condition. The comparison can locate a question. It cannot answer it for him.
notes: Based on Essays III.9, rendered freely. Additions are permitted by the stated rule and are not treated as counterexamples. The discussion concerns the unresolved tension introduced by deletions and replacements.

zh.title: 我如今和我方才
zh.deck: 改过很多次，不等于已经知道哪一个自己更好。

paragraphs: 还是《论虚妄》这一章。这一篇只看一句话。
在一五八八年的印面上，他说的是：从头一批书出版到现在，我又老了八年，可我怀疑自己长进了一寸没有。
这句话本身已经够坦白。到了波尔多本上，它又成了一处反复落笔的地方。

sections.heading: 这一句周围的几重手迹
paragraphs: 数目是一处。八年被划掉，旁边写了七年。
年份又是一处。他添过一条小注，点明那是一五八〇年；那条小注后来也被划掉了。
原句的大部分印字上有了删线，他另写了新句：我头一批书出在一五八〇年。此后经了很长一段时日，我是老了；可要说长进，我确然没有一寸。
新句内部还有修改。我没有，又被改成了我确然没有。右边栏上，则另有一整段话。
这些动作可以并排列出：改过年份，补过小注，取消过小注，重写过句子，在新句里再改，也在页边接着写。这里列的是痕迹的种类，不是一份已经排定的日程。

sections.heading: 能看出什么，看不出什么
paragraphs: 同一处已经写下的字，后来才可能被划去。这种局部的先后，有时能从痕迹本身认出来。可不能因此把整张纸上每一次落笔都排成年月分明的一列。
哪条挨着哪条，哪条压在哪条上面，是一种证据；哪一笔落在哪一年，是另一件事。同一处替换，也可以把划和写算成两件事，或算成一次修改。数目跟着分类走，不是纸上天然长着的。
页边添上的那一段也不是一句短注。它自成一段，内部又有增删。新添上去的文字，也没有得到一次写定、不再经手的待遇。
不用替它编出一条完整的先后，一件事已经看得见：一句说自己未必长进的话，仍让他一次次回到纸上。

sections.heading: 也不是全靠他一个人
paragraphs: 顺带说一件常被漏掉的事。
那册书上不只有他的手。编者辨认出三处玛丽·德·古尔奈的代笔。其中一处在第四十二叶背面，蒙田写下开头那个词，其余由她接着记下他的口授。
所以，这册书不能被想成一个人关在塔楼里、从头到尾独自落下的笔迹。有过另一个人在旁边，有过另一只执笔的手。

sections.heading: 页边那一句
paragraphs: 那段话里，有这样一句：我如今和我方才，确是两个人。可哪一个更好，我说不上来。
前半句，是他这本书一贯的话头。要紧的是后半句。
他大可以写成：我如今比我方才明白些。一个在自己的旧书上改了几年的人这样说，听起来并不突兀。
他留下的却不是这一句。

sections.heading: 替三年前的自己收摊子
paragraphs: 这件事人人做过。回头去收拾自己几年前留下的一个摊子，常常看得见当时看不见的东西：哪一步想岔了，哪一句不该说。
而这不担保这一次就看准了。同一只回来的手，既可能把它改好，也可能把它改坏。改坏的那些，也是当时觉得改对了，才落下去的。
蒙田在这一处动了那么多手，页边却还留着这个意思：两个人是两个人，谁更好不知道。这不是说修改都没有用，是说修改过，和已经能够替自己判定进步，并不是同一件事。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 首刊在一五八〇年。今天藏在波尔多的这一册，是一五八八年的印本，保存的是他在那之后几年里继续做的事。
一个人回到自己写过的话上。年份、小注、整句、页边，各处都留下了动笔的痕迹。我们不必知道每一笔的日期，才看得见他没有就此停手。
而他留在页边的，不是一张比从前更好的凭据。是一句说自己分不清哪一个更好的话。

zh.aside: SAE 的意义论里有一句，可以放在这条边注旁边：成长登记的是新取得了一种真实的处理方式，不是越来越接近一个完成的自己。按这个说法，一个在旧书上改了几年的人，并不欠自己一句我比从前明白。并读所能保留的是这个区别，不是把蒙田后来留下的每一笔都登记成成长。
notes: 据《随笔集》III.9译述。局部先写后划不等于全页各次修改的完整时间顺序；文中并列描述手迹，不据空间位置虚构写作次序。
本篇所述删改据波尔多本叶面0433的手稿转录；一五九五年版仅供对读，不视为这些改笔的证据。

en.title: The Man I Am, the Man I Just Was
en.deck: Returning to the page is one thing. Knowing that the later self is better is another.

paragraphs: We are still in Of Vanity. This time, the point of departure is a single sentence.
In the printing of 1588, Montaigne says that he has aged eight years since his first books appeared, but doubts whether he has improved an inch.
It is frank enough already. In the Bordeaux Copy, it becomes a place to which his pen repeatedly returns.

sections.heading: Several kinds of intervention
paragraphs: There is a change to the number. Eight is crossed out, and seven is supplied beside it.
There is a change involving the date. A small addition specifies 1580; that note is itself cancelled.

Most of the printed sentence has been struck through, and a new sentence written: My first books appeared in 1580. A long stretch of time has passed since then. I have grown older; I have certainly not grown an inch better.
The replacement has its own revision. I have not becomes I have certainly not. A further passage occupies the right margin.

The actions can be placed beside one another: a number changed, a note added, a note cancelled, a sentence rewritten, new wording revised, more writing supplied in the margin. This is an inventory of marks, not a calendar of their making.

sections.heading: What the paper can tell us
paragraphs: Words must be written before those same words can be crossed out. A local sequence of that kind can sometimes be read in the marks themselves. It does not follow that every intervention across the page can be arranged into a complete chronology.

What lies beside what, and what is written over what, are one kind of evidence. The year in which a stroke was made is another matter. Even a replacement can be counted as two actions—deleting and writing—or as one revision. The total follows the categories we choose; it is not a number naturally inscribed in the paper.

The added marginal passage is more than a brief note. It is a passage in its own right, with further additions and deletions inside it. Being newly written did not exempt it from being worked on again.
We do not need to invent a complete sequence to see what is remarkable. A sentence doubting his own improvement continued to bring him back to the page.

sections.heading: Not only his hand
paragraphs: One detail is often lost in the familiar picture of Montaigne at work.

The handwriting in this copy is not entirely his. Editors identify three passages written by Marie de Gournay. In one of them, on folio 42 verso, Montaigne wrote the opening word and she continued, taking down his dictation.
So this volume should not be imagined as the uninterrupted work of a solitary man shut in a tower. At certain moments, another person was beside him. Another hand held the pen.

sections.heading: The sentence in the margin
paragraphs: The marginal passage includes a thought that can be put like this: the man I am now and the man I was a moment ago are certainly two different people. Which is better, I cannot say.
The first half is familiar territory in the Essays. The second half is what matters here.
He could have said that the present man understood a little more. Coming from someone who had spent years revising his own book, the claim would hardly have sounded extravagant.
It is not the claim he left on this page.

sections.heading: Tidying up after an earlier self
paragraphs: We have all returned to something left behind by an earlier version of ourselves. Now we can see the mistaken turn, the sentence we should not have spoken. It is tempting to take that clearer view of an old mistake as evidence that this time we are seeing clearly.
It is no guarantee. The hand that comes back may improve the work or make it worse. The changes that make it worse are often made with exactly the same confidence as the ones that help.

Montaigne works repeatedly on this passage and still leaves room for the distinction: there are two people; which is better is not settled. That does not make revision pointless. It separates having revised from being entitled to certify one's own progress.

sections.heading: No certificate of improvement
paragraphs: The first publication was in 1580. The volume now in Bordeaux was printed in 1588 and preserves work done during the remaining years of Montaigne's life.
A man returns to words he has written. A date, a note, a sentence, a margin: the marks of further work are there. We need not date every stroke to see that he did not stop.
But what he leaves in the margin is not a certificate that he has become better. It is a sentence saying that he cannot tell which of the two men is better.

en.aside: SAE's account of meaning offers a distinction worth setting beside the marginal sentence: growth records the acquisition of a real way of responding, not an approach towards a completed self. On that account, a man who spends years revising his book does not owe himself a declaration that he is wiser than before. The comparison preserves a distinction. It does not automatically enter every later pen stroke in a ledger of growth.
notes: Based on Essays III.9, rendered freely. A local sequence of writing and cancellation is distinguished from a complete chronology of interventions across the page. Spatial arrangement alone does not establish that chronology.
The revisions described here follow the Bordeaux Copy’s manuscript transcription for leaf 0433. The 1595 text is supplied for comparison, not as evidence of these pen marks.
